abstract: We study the areas of the cells determined by an arrangement $\mathcal{A}$ of $n$ distinct great circles on the unit sphere, with no three concurrent. Let $m(\mathcal{A})$ and $M(\mathcal{A})$ denote the smallest and largest cell areas, respectively. Our first result is the bound \[ m(\mathcal{A})\le \frac{C_*+O(n^{-3/4})}{n^2}, \qquad C_*=7.0666071493\ldots , \] where the implied constant is absolute. This improves the coefficient $\pi^2$ obtained from classical polygonal perimeter estimates. We also prove that $M(\mathcal{A})/m(\mathcal{A})>13$ for all sufficiently large $n$, improving the bound $7.43$ of L.~Fejes T\'oth. The main tool is a perimeter inequality for planar polygons which takes account of their exterior angles. We combine this with a positive semidefinite kernel on the sphere and use gnomonic projection to obtain bounds for spherical cells.
hook: In any arrangement of n great circles, some cell has area at most about 7.07 over n squared.

summary: For n great circles on a sphere with no three meeting at a point, the smallest cell area is bounded by roughly 7.0666 divided by n squared, improving the older constant pi squared. The largest cell is also shown to exceed 13 times the smallest for large n. The proof uses a new perimeter inequality for polygons and a positive semidefinite kernel; the bounds are upper limits and not shown to be tight.
title: Small cells in great-circle arrangements
